issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
Kai is a 55-year-old man of Oceania descent, a nanny by profession, who came to therapy at the urging of his sister. He had been divorced for nearly a decade and lived alone in a small apartment, a space he had come to think of as a kind of holding cell. He was referred by his primary care doctor after a routine visit during which he broke down sobbing when asked about his sleep. He scored a 65 on the PCL-5, and the clinical picture that emerged over the first few sessions was one of profound, unprocessed grief and a deep sense of personal failure.

The event that had shattered Kai's life occurred three years earlier. He had been the live-in nanny for a family with two young children, a boy and a girl, whom he had cared for since infancy. One afternoon, while he was preparing their lunch, a neighbor's dog, a large animal that had never shown aggression before, got into the backyard through a broken latch. Kai heard the children screaming and ran outside. He saw the dog on top of the four-year-old boy, its jaws clamped around the child's arm. Kai grabbed a metal rake and struck the dog repeatedly, shouting, trying to drive it off. By the time the dog released the boy and fled, the child's arm was mangled, the bone visible through torn flesh. The boy survived, but underwent multiple surgeries and would have permanent scarring and nerve damage. Kai had been the one to hold the child, to apply pressure to the wound, to scream for help. He had done everything right in the moment, but that was not how he experienced it.

What haunted Kai was not the event itself, but the aftermath in his own mind. When he tried to tell anyone what had happened-his sister, a former colleague, a therapist he briefly saw-he would lose the thread. His sentences would become tangled. He would start describing the sound of the boy's scream, a high, wet, tearing noise that he could still hear in his head when he closed his eyes, and then he would stop. He could not finish. The story would collapse into silence, and he would feel the grief rise like a wave, overwhelming, oceanic, leaving him gasping. He had come to believe that he could not explain what happened because he was too weak to bear it. He was a weak person. That belief had calcified over the months.

He also began to feel that he was no longer a person. In the months after the attack, he noticed that when he looked in the mirror, he did not recognize himself. He felt like an object, a thing that had been present at a terrible moment, a piece of furniture that had failed in its function. He had been the protector, and he had failed. The boy had been hurt. Kai should have checked the latch. He should have been faster. He should have done something else, something more. The idea that he had failed to protect the child was not a thought he entertained; it was a fact, as solid as the scar on the boy's arm.

Kai's work as a nanny became impossible. He quit the job the week after the attack, unable to face the family, unable to look at the boy's arm in a cast. He tried to take on other nanny positions, but he could not manage them. The triggers were everywhere. A child's bare arm, especially a small one, would make his stomach turn. The sight of a child's elbow, the curve of a wrist, the soft skin of a toddler's leg-these body parts, so familiar from years of care, now carried the full force of the memory. He also found himself unable to be around reminders of victims in general. A news story about a child hurt in an accident, a charity appeal for a sick infant, a conversation about a neighbor's lost pet-anything involving someone who had been harmed would send him into a spiral. And talk of loss was the worst. When friends or family mentioned someone who had lost a loved one, Kai would feel a physical pain in his chest, a grief that was not his own but felt as though it were, and he would have to excuse himself.

Over the next two years, Kai's world shrank. He took a job as a night cleaner in an office building, working alone, seeing no one. He avoided parks, playgrounds, and any street where he might see a child. He stopped answering calls from his sister because she often talked about her own children, and he could not bear it. He had come to believe that he was dangerous to be around, that his failure to protect made him a kind of contamination. He was certain that if he let himself feel the full force of his grief, he would never stop crying, and so he tried not to feel at all. But the memories came anyway, unbidden, with the sound of that scream in his head, and the grief would crash over him in his empty apartment at night.

What finally brought Kai to seek help was not a realization about his own suffering, but a practical failure. He had started to miss work because he could not get out of bed. His sister threatened to call for a welfare check. He agreed to see a therapist because he was terrified of being hospitalized, of being seen as crazy, of being locked away. What he hoped for, he said in a low voice during his first session, was to stop feeling like a ghost. He did not expect to feel better. He did not expect to forgive himself. He just wanted to be able to get through a day without hearing that scream, and without feeling that he was no longer a person at all.
